strengths: Novel and well-motivated framework addressing the genuine gap of treating modular two-stage pipelines as black boxes; the residual decomposition enabling stage-wise uncertainty attribution is conceptually clean and practically useful

Solid theoretical contributions including coverage guarantees for separate quantiles (Theorem 1), existence of ideal scaling parameters (Proposition 2), risk-controlled selection via FWER (Theorem 2), and long-run adaptive guarantees (Proposition 3)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with synthetic experiments carefully isolating upstream/downstream/covariate shifts, two real-world datasets with interpretable diagnostics (Figures 12-13 showing how scaling parameters adapt to different shocks), and extensive ablation studies

Clear interpretability benefits: method identifies which pipeline stage drives uncertainty and enables targeted interventions (demonstrated by selective retraining example showing 24.6→25.3 width reduction)
Flexible framework with multiple formulations (separate vs scaled quantiles) and extensions discussed (multi-stage, auxiliary data, φ-mixing sequences)
weaknesses: Severe practical limitation to two-stage models: extension to K stages (Appendix C.4) has exponential complexity in |Λ|, making it impractical for common 3+ stage pipelines; proposed top-k heuristic lacks theoretical justification

Strong intermediate variable observability requirement (x must be observed for all data points) is frequently violated in practice when x is latent, noisy, or delayed; no analysis of robustness to partial/noisy observations

Significant theory-practice gap for main method (Definition 4 scaled quantiles): lacks finite-sample coverage guarantees for arbitrary (a,b); Proposition 2 only shows existence without constructive method; Theorem 2 provides weaker conditional guarantees (coverage ≥ 1-α-τ with probability 1-δ rather than deterministic 1-α)

Excessive conservatism in benign settings: Table 4 shows 0.94-0.98 coverage when targeting 0.90 (IID linear); intervals 15-34% wider than baselines (Tables 4, Figure 3 automobile data); conservatism stems from FWER but limits practical utility, requiring tolerance parameter τ as additional hyperparameter

Limited practical improvements on real data: automobile dataset (Figure 3) shows comparable/wider intervals than ACI despite better coverage; stock dataset shows incremental improvements; benefits primarily manifest on artificial symmetric shifts, while covariate shifts show no advantage over baselines (Appendix D.3.7)

Abstention presented as diagnostic but unvalidated: method produces empty Λ_val under large shifts; no analysis of abstention frequency or correlation with whether retraining is actually necessary; appears to be reframing inability to predict as a feature

Adaptive algorithm components are ad-hoc: SELECTLAMBDA (Appendix B.5) compares recent averages ΔR̄₁ vs R̄₂ without principled justification; adjusting c_t, d_t to expand Λ_val is heuristic; parameter bounds [-η, 1+η] appear arbitrary

High hyperparameter complexity with 8 parameters (α, τ, δ, γ, η, c, d, k) and significant sensitivity: coverage varies from 0.595-0.880 across γ ∈ {0.01, 0.1} (Table 8); no principled guidance for practitioners on setting these a priori

Limited real-world evaluation: only 2 real datasets (both forecasting); no comparison to simple baseline of retraining entire pipeline when coverage drops; missing applications in other domains (classification, anomaly detection)

Exchangeability assumptions weaker than presented: Theorem 2 requires IID calibration but adaptive method uses sliding windows; Section C.2 φ-mixing extension significantly loosens guarantees; practical guarantees weaker for non-exchangeable real data

strengths: Novel problem formulation addressing a genuine gap in conformal prediction: stage-wise uncertainty attribution in multi-stage pipelines
Sound theoretical framework with multiple coverage guarantees (Theorems 5.2, 6.1) and extensions to φ-mixing and multi-stage settings
Comprehensive experimental validation across synthetic and real-world datasets with extensive ablation studies and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis
Practical diagnostic value: identifies which pipeline stages drive prediction uncertainty, enabling targeted interventions
Robust coverage under asymmetric stage-wise distribution shifts, demonstrated convincingly on controlled synthetic experiments and real data (automobile supply chain COVID-19 shift)
Methodologically complete with FWER-based parameter selection, adaptive variant with long-run guarantees, and practical hyperparameter guidelines
Well-organized presentation with effective visualizations (e.g., Figures 16-17 showing residual component adaptation) and extensive appendices
weaknesses: Proposition 5.5 establishes existence of ideal scaling parameters (a*, b*) but provides no characterization or construction method; gap between existence and practical FWER selection lacks theoretical elegance

Coverage-efficiency tradeoff inadequately analyzed: method produces unnecessarily wide intervals and frequent abstention (Λval = ∅) under severe shifts; covariate shifts (Section D.4.7) show no advantage over baselines, suggesting specialized applicability
Problem scope limited to two-stage models with observable intermediate representations; multi-stage extension (Definition C.4) faces computational explosion and practical infeasibility
Residual decomposition captures upstream error indirectly through downstream model lens; ∆R₁ doesn't isolate upstream error in nonlinear scenarios; upper bound property R ≤ ∆R₁ + R₂ can be loose
IID assumption on Scal in Theorem 6.1 conflicts with adaptive sliding window approach used in practice; φ-mixing extension (C.2) only sketched
Tolerance parameter τ needed to match baseline efficiency in IID settings (Tables 5) somewhat undermines 'risk-controlled' framing; practical benefits require τ ∈ [0.03, 0.05]

Numerous hyperparameters with somewhat arbitrary defaults (γ=0.01, η=0.01, δ=0.3, k=100) despite ablations; FWER algorithm choice (Bonferroni vs. fixed sequence testing) significantly impacts results but guidance is limited

Real-world automobile experiment shows comparable mean width to baselines (18.957 vs. ACI 15.696) despite claimed robustness; gains appear specialized to stage-wise shifts rather than general distribution shifts
